summary: Fire Rings: NASA’s 25-year fire record, harmonized once so nobody else has to. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fire differently: joined naively, fire appears to jump +199% in 2012 in Punjab, although only the satellite changed. Every researcher, agency or app that uses NASA fire data has to solve this first. We solved it once, validated it, and give it away: a ready-to-use, open harmonized record (CSV, Parquet, open API, no key) that updates itself daily. We count fire-days on ~36 km² hexagons and convert VIIRS into MODIS-equivalent units, tested on years the method never saw (1.8 to 9.2% error; the 2012 jump disappears). On top, we built a burning activity calendar for 9 regions, an “is this month normal?” comparison against the 2003 to 2022 median, harmonized and raw hotspot downloads, a fire-likelihood model, and Fire Watch, where an agent checks each alert with detection times, NASA burned area and a geostationary satellite. On raw data, 128 of 243 alerts since 2012 are fake. With MODIS ending in 2027, Fire Rings is the bridge between NASA’s fire data and the people building on it.
details:
The idea
A harmonized NASA fire layer anyone can build on. Every researcher, agency, insurer or app developer who wants to use NASA’s 25 years of fire data first hits the same wall: MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fire differently, so the record breaks in 2012. Fire Rings removes that wall once, for everyone. We harmonize MODIS and VIIRS into one consistent monthly record from 2001 to today, validate it publicly (out-of-sample tests, a validation report, uncertainty for every month), and publish it as open data (CSV, Parquet) and a free API with no key, refreshed daily. Others can skip straight to their own idea; our companion app (https://fire-rings-apps.vercel.app) is built only on that public API, as proof. The current record covers 9 regions (Punjab and Haryana, Madagascar, SE Australia, Mauritius incl. Rodrigues, Northern Territory savanna, Northeast India, Tanzania, Sudan, Mato Grosso), and the world archive is ready for more.

How it works

  1. We read the FIRMS archive (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m from S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) and near-real-time data.
  2. We remove low-confidence detections and non-fire heat sources (volcanoes, factories, gas flares, offshore platforms) using FIRMS labels plus our own mask of persistent hot spots.
  3. We count fire-days: an H3 hexagon (~36 km²) with at least one detection on a local solar day.
  4. For each region and month we fit the ratio of MODIS to VIIRS fire-days from July 2012 to December 2019, with shrinkage for low-fire months, and convert VIIRS into MODIS-equivalent units, with bridges for Terra-only years and for NOAA-20 after S-NPP.
  5. 500 bootstrap runs give a 90% range for every month.
  6. A region is published only if it passes out-of-sample tests: leave-one-year-out error under 20% (actual 1.8 to 9.2%) and no remaining jump at 2012 (Punjab +199% → +3.1%, MODIS alone +4.2%).

Features

  • A fire-ring calendar (each ring a year)
  • Seasonality and yearly charts
  • An “is this month normal?” gauge vs the 2003 to 2022 median
  • A hexagon map with a draw-a-box tool
  • Downloads of the harmonized fire-days CSV and raw NASA hotspots
  • An open API with no key
  • Fire Watch: it applies fixed published rules every day. An agent then checks each flagged month with detection times, NASA MCD64A1 burned area and NOAA GOES geostationary data, and gives a verdict (Real change / Detection issue likely / Unclear / Not checkable yet) that is saved in the data and API. A language model only explains verified numbers.
  • A fire-likelihood model (gradient-boosted trees): it ranks hexagons for the coming month. On unseen years, the top 10% of hexagons capture 32% of next month’s fire vs 28% for the usual season. It retrains monthly and is published only if it beats the baseline.

Benefits

  • It removes fake alerts (128 of 243 on raw data)
  • It reveals real drops hidden by the satellite switch
  • It gives fire services, air-quality agencies, insurers and researchers a fair 25-year baseline as MODIS ends in 2027

Local feedback
A Mauritian environmental engineer we consulted (anonymous at their request) saw these uses:

  • monitoring sugarcane burning at harvest time
  • wildfires in nature reserves and on the drier northern mountains
  • open waste burning
    They suggested the Ministry of Environment, Forestry Services and conservation organisations as users. They also raised honest limits: the coarse resolution for a small island, cloud cover, and limited local training data. Combining several satellites reduces cloud gaps, and data from similar island states could help.

Tools
Python (DuckDB, Polars, PyArrow, H3, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn), React + TypeScript + Vite, MapLibre GL, D3, Vercel (hosting and serverless functions), GitHub Actions (daily updates, monthly retraining), Google Gemini (explanations only), and Claude Code (coding assistant).
